--- title: "Data wrangling with _dplyr_" author: - name: Software Carpentry - name: Jelmer Poelstra orcid: 0000-0002-3514-7462 email: poelstra.1@osu.edu affiliation: - name: CFAES Bioinformatics Core, Ohio State University url: https://go.osu.edu/bioinformatics-core date: 2026-06-08 date-modified: last-modified engine: knitr format: live-html: theme: yeti syntax-highlighting: atom-one css: - styles.css - include/webex.css include-after-body: include/webex.js toc: true number-sections: true number-depth: 3 grid: body-width: 800px webr: cell-options: autorun: true --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell context='setup'} ```{webr} #| label: setup #| include: false #| context: setup library(gapminder) library(dplyr) ``` ::: -------
## Introduction ### What we'll cover Many of the most common data analysis tasks involve working with **tabular data**, i.e. data with rows and columns. In this session, you'll learn to work with tabular data in R using the _dplyr_ package. For example, you'll see how to subset, manipulate and summarize a dataset, the kinds of tasks commonly referred to as "data wrangling". Such data processing is often essential before you can move on to say, data visualization (next session of this workshop) or statistical analyses. ### Setting up Use a new script for this session, much like we did for the previous one: 1. _Open a new R script_ (Click the **`+`** symbol in toolbar at the top, then click `R Script`)^[ Or Click `File` => `New file` => `R Script`.]. 2. _Save the script_ straight away as `data-wrangling.R` -- you can save it anywhere you like, though it is probably best to save it in a folder specifically for this workshop. 3. If you want the section headers as comments in your script, like in the script I am showing you in the live session, then copy-and-paste the following into your script:
Section headers for your script _(Click to expand)_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # TODO - UPDATE # 1 - Introduction ---------------------------------------------------- # 1.4 - Loading the tidyverse # 2 - The gapminder dataset ------------------------------------------ # Challenge 1 # 3 - arrange() ------------------------------------------------------- # Challenge 2 # 4 - filter() -------------------------------------------------------- # 4.1 - Filter based on one condition # 4.2 - Filter based on multiple conditions # 5 - The pipe -------------------------------------------------------- # Challenge 3 # Challenge 4 # 6 - mutate() -------------------------------------------------------- # Challenge 5 # 7 - summarize() ----------------------------------------------------- # Challenge 6 ``` :::
### The _dplyr_ package and the tidyverse One of R's most powerful features is its ability to deal with **tabular data**: data with rows and columns like you are familiar with from Excel spreadsheets and so on --- for example:
::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.801 8425333 779.4453 2 Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.332 9240934 820.8530 3 Afghanistan Asia 1962 31.997 10267083 853.1007 4 Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.020 11537966 836.1971 5 Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.088 13079460 739.9811 6 Afghanistan Asia 1977 38.438 14880372 786.1134 ``` ::: ::: In R, tabular data is stored in a data structure called "**data frame**". The [_dplyr_](https://cran.r-project.org/package=dplyr) package provides very useful functions for **manipulating data in data frames**. In this session, we'll cover these commonly used _dplyr_ functions: - `arrange()` to change the order of rows (i.e., to sort a data frame) - `filter()` to keep only a subset of rows - `mutate()` to manipulate columns and create new columns - `summarize()` to compute data summaries across rows _dplyr_ has many more functions. Some of these are more advanced than those we'll cover today, while others are conceptually simpler (e.g. `rename()` to change column names and `select()` to select columns), and we encourage you to [explore](#bonus-material-for-self-study) these [on your own](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/dplyr.html). _dplyr_ belongs to a **family of R packages for data science called the** ["tidyverse"](https://www.tidyverse.org).** Another tidyverse package we'll cover in today's workshop is _ggplot2_ for making plots. ### Loading the tidyverse All core tidyverse packages can be installed and loaded with a single command. Since you should already have _installed_ the tidyverse^[ If not: run `install.packages("tidyverse")` now. ], you only need to _load_ it, which you do as follows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ✔ dplyr 1.2.1 ✔ readr 2.2.0 ✔ forcats 1.0.1 ✔ stringr 1.6.0 ✔ ggplot2 4.0.3 ✔ tibble 3.3.1 ✔ lubridate 1.9.5 ✔ tidyr 1.3.2 ✔ purrr 1.2.2 ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ℹ Use the conflicted package () to force all conflicts to become errors ``` ::: ::: The output tells you which packages have been loaded as part of the tidyverse. (For now, you don't have to pay attention to or worry about the ["Conflicts" section](#function-name-conflicts).) ## The `gapminder` dataset In this session and the next one on data visualization, we will work with the `gapminder` dataset, which contains statistics such as population size for different countries across five-year intervals. This dataset is available in a package of the same name, which you already should have installed as well^[ If not: run `install.packages("gapminder")` now. ]. To load the package into your current R session: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # (Unlike with the tidyverse, no output is expected when you load gapminder) library(gapminder) ``` ::: Take a look at the `gapminder` data frame that is now available to you: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.8 8425333 779. 2 Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.3 9240934 821. 3 Afghanistan Asia 1962 32.0 10267083 853. 4 Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.0 11537966 836. 5 Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.1 13079460 740. 6 Afghanistan Asia 1977 38.4 14880372 786. 7 Afghanistan Asia 1982 39.9 12881816 978. 8 Afghanistan Asia 1987 40.8 13867957 852. 9 Afghanistan Asia 1992 41.7 16317921 649. 10 Afghanistan Asia 1997 41.8 22227415 635. # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: The first 10 rows are printed, with the following columns: | column name | data type | meaning | |---|---|------| | `country` | `factor` (``) | Country | | `continent` | `factor` (``) | Continent that the country is in | | `year` | `integer` (``) | Focal year for the stats in the next columns | | `lifeExp` | `integer` (``) | Mean life expectancy in years | | `pop` | `integer` (``) | Population size | | `gdpPercap` | `double` (``) | Per-capita GDP | : {.striped}
Two columns are of type `factor`, [an alternative to](./2_vectors.qmd#factors) `character` commonly used for categorical data. You can also use the `View()` function to look at the data frame. This will open a new tab in your editor pane with a spreadsheet-like look and feel: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} View(gapminder) # (Should display the dataset in an editor pane tab) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} In the `head()` output above, the `gapminder` data frame is referred to as a *"tibble"*, which is just a slight variation on data frames from the tidyverse^[ The main difference is the nicer default printing behavior of tibbles: e.g. the data types of columns are shown, and only a limited number of rows are printed.]. ::: ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Challenge 1: Explore the `gapminder` dataset** TODO ::: ## `arrange()` The `arrange()` function is like sorting functionality in Excel: it changes the order of rows based on the values in one or more columns. It will always rearrange the order of rows as a whole, never just of individual columns since that would scramble the data. `gapminder` is currently first sorted alphabetically by `country`, and next by `year`. But you may, for example, want to sort by population size instead, which you can do with `arrange()` as follows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gm_arranged <- arrange(.data = gapminder, pop) ``` ::: Before we take a look at the result, let's break down the syntax of the `arrange()` function: - The first argument is the data frame to be sorted, which we specify with the `.data` argument. - The second argument is the column to sort by, which we specify without an argument name. ::: callout-note Like all _dplyr_ functions, `arrange()` outputs a new data frame, and **does not modify the input data frame.** In this case, we chose to assign the output to a new object called `gm_arranged`.
[{{< fa comments >}}]{style="color: darkgreen;"} What would have happened if we had assigned the output to `gapminder`? In that case, the original dataframe would have been overwritten with the sorted version.
::: Now let's look at the result of the sorting: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gm_arranged ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1952 46.5 60011 880. 2 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1957 48.9 61325 861. 3 Djibouti Africa 1952 34.8 63149 2670. 4 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1962 51.9 65345 1072. 5 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1967 54.4 70787 1385. 6 Djibouti Africa 1957 37.3 71851 2865. 7 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1972 56.5 76595 1533. 8 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1977 58.6 86796 1738. 9 Djibouti Africa 1962 39.7 89898 3021. 10 Sao Tome and Principe Africa 1982 60.4 98593 1890. # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: Sorting can help you find observations with the smallest or largest values for a certain column: above, we see that the smallest population size in the dataset is _Sao Tome and Principe_ in 1952. Default sorting is from **small to large**, as seen above . To sort in reverse order, use the `desc()` (descending) helper function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange(.data = gapminder, desc(pop)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 China Asia 2007 73.0 1318683096 4959. 2 China Asia 2002 72.0 1280400000 3119. 3 China Asia 1997 70.4 1230075000 2289. 4 China Asia 1992 68.7 1164970000 1656. 5 India Asia 2007 64.7 1110396331 2452. 6 China Asia 1987 67.3 1084035000 1379. 7 India Asia 2002 62.9 1034172547 1747. 8 China Asia 1982 65.5 1000281000 962. 9 India Asia 1997 61.8 959000000 1459. 10 China Asia 1977 64.0 943455000 741. # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple'} Here, we didn't assign the output to a new object, so it was just printed to screen. We'll keep doing that for the rest of the examples in this session, so we can more easily see the results of the operations we are performing. ::: Finally, you may want to sort by multiple columns, where ties in the first column are broken by a second column (and so on). Do this by simply listing the columns in the appropriate order: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sort first by continent, then by country: arrange(.data = gapminder, continent, country) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Algeria Africa 1952 43.1 9279525 2449. 2 Algeria Africa 1957 45.7 10270856 3014. 3 Algeria Africa 1962 48.3 11000948 2551. 4 Algeria Africa 1967 51.4 12760499 3247. 5 Algeria Africa 1972 54.5 14760787 4183. 6 Algeria Africa 1977 58.0 17152804 4910. 7 Algeria Africa 1982 61.4 20033753 5745. 8 Algeria Africa 1987 65.8 23254956 5681. 9 Algeria Africa 1992 67.7 26298373 5023. 10 Algeria Africa 1997 69.2 29072015 4797. # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: Pay attention to the syntax: additional columns to sort by are additional arguments to the function, not part of the same argument. Other _dplyr_ functions work equivalently in this regard. :::exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Challenge 2: `arrange()`** One observation (row) in the `gapminder` dataset has the highest per-capita GDP. Which line of code would you use to find out which row that is? Try it, and report which row (which country and year) you found. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Quiz
#### {{< fa circle-info >}} Explanation While both the first and third options will give you the row with the highest per-capita GDP, the first option will also sort the entire dataset by year and country, which is not necessary to answer the question. You'll want to sort descendingly by `gdpPercap` to get the row with the highest value at the top. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange(.data = gapminder, desc(gdpPercap)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Kuwait Asia 1957 58.0 212846 113523. 2 Kuwait Asia 1972 67.7 841934 109348. 3 Kuwait Asia 1952 55.6 160000 108382. 4 Kuwait Asia 1962 60.5 358266 95458. 5 Kuwait Asia 1967 64.6 575003 80895. 6 Kuwait Asia 1977 69.3 1140357 59265. 7 Norway Europe 2007 80.2 4627926 49357. 8 Kuwait Asia 2007 77.6 2505559 47307. 9 Singapore Asia 2007 80.0 4553009 47143. 10 Norway Europe 2002 79.0 4535591 44684. # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: Kuwait in 1957 had the highest per-capita GDP in the dataset, at $113,523. ::: ::: ## `filter()` The `filter()` function outputs only those rows that satisfy one or more conditions. It is similar to Filter functionality in Excel. ### Filter based on one condition This first `filter()` example outputs only rows for which the life expectancy exceeds 80 years (remember, each row represents a country in a given year): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filter(.data = gapminder, lifeExp > 80) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 21 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Australia Oceania 2002 80.4 19546792 30688. 2 Australia Oceania 2007 81.2 20434176 34435. 3 Canada Americas 2007 80.7 33390141 36319. 4 France Europe 2007 80.7 61083916 30470. 5 Hong Kong, China Asia 2002 81.5 6762476 30209. 6 Hong Kong, China Asia 2007 82.2 6980412 39725. 7 Iceland Europe 2002 80.5 288030 31163. 8 Iceland Europe 2007 81.8 301931 36181. 9 Israel Asia 2007 80.7 6426679 25523. 10 Italy Europe 2002 80.2 57926999 27968. # ℹ 11 more rows ``` ::: :::
[{{< fa comments >}}]{style="color: darkgreen;"} How many rows were output? As is printed in the first line of the output, 21 rows were output.
As the example above demonstrated, `filter()` **outputs rows that satisfy the condition(s)** you specify. These conditions don't have to be based on numeric comparisons: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Only keep rows where the value in the 'continent' column is 'Europe': filter(.data = gapminder, continent == "Europe") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 360 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Albania Europe 1952 55.2 1282697 1601. 2 Albania Europe 1957 59.3 1476505 1942. 3 Albania Europe 1962 64.8 1728137 2313. 4 Albania Europe 1967 66.2 1984060 2760. 5 Albania Europe 1972 67.7 2263554 3313. 6 Albania Europe 1977 68.9 2509048 3533. 7 Albania Europe 1982 70.4 2780097 3631. 8 Albania Europe 1987 72 3075321 3739. 9 Albania Europe 1992 71.6 3326498 2497. 10 Albania Europe 1997 73.0 3428038 3193. # ℹ 350 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning appearance='simple'} Remember to use _two_ equals signs `==` to test for equality! ::: ### Filter based on multiple conditions It's also possible to filter based on multiple conditions. For example, you may want to see which countries in Asia had a life expectancy greater than 80 years: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filter(.data = gapminder, continent == "Asia", lifeExp > 80) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 6 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Hong Kong, China Asia 2002 81.5 6762476 30209. 2 Hong Kong, China Asia 2007 82.2 6980412 39725. 3 Israel Asia 2007 80.7 6426679 25523. 4 Japan Asia 1997 80.7 125956499 28817. 5 Japan Asia 2002 82 127065841 28605. 6 Japan Asia 2007 82.6 127467972 31656. ``` ::: ::: Like above, by default, multiple conditions are combined using a Boolean ***AND***. In other words, in a given row, _each_ condition must be met to output the row. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} #### What about a Boolean ***OR***? _(Click to expand)_ If you want to combine conditions using a Boolean ***OR***, where only one of the conditions needs to be met, use a `|` (vertical bar) between the conditions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Keep rows with a high life expectancy and/or a high GDP: filter(.data = gapminder, lifeExp > 80 | gdpPercap > 100000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 24 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Australia Oceania 2002 80.4 19546792 30688. 2 Australia Oceania 2007 81.2 20434176 34435. 3 Canada Americas 2007 80.7 33390141 36319. 4 France Europe 2007 80.7 61083916 30470. 5 Hong Kong, China Asia 2002 81.5 6762476 30209. 6 Hong Kong, China Asia 2007 82.2 6980412 39725. 7 Iceland Europe 2002 80.5 288030 31163. 8 Iceland Europe 2007 81.8 301931 36181. 9 Israel Asia 2007 80.7 6426679 25523. 10 Italy Europe 2002 80.2 57926999 27968. # ℹ 14 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ## The pipe (`|>`) Examples so far applied a single _dplyr_ function to a data frame. But in practice, it's common to use several consecutive _dplyr_ functions to wrangle a dataframe into the format you want. For example, you may want to filter rows and then sort the result. You could do that as follows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gm_filt <- filter(.data = gapminder, lifeExp < 50, year > 2000) arrange(.data = gm_filt, desc(pop)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 42 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Nigeria Africa 2007 46.9 135031164 2014. 2 Nigeria Africa 2002 46.6 119901274 1615. 3 Congo, Dem. Rep. Africa 2007 46.5 64606759 278. 4 Congo, Dem. Rep. Africa 2002 45.0 55379852 241. 5 South Africa Africa 2007 49.3 43997828 9270. 6 Tanzania Africa 2002 49.7 34593779 899. 7 Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.8 31889923 975. 8 Afghanistan Asia 2002 42.1 25268405 727. 9 Uganda Africa 2002 47.8 24739869 928. 10 Mozambique Africa 2007 42.1 19951656 824. # ℹ 32 more rows ``` ::: ::: And you could go on along these lines, successively creating new objects that you then use for the next step. But there is a more elegent way of dong this, directly sending ("piping") output from one function into the next function with the **pipe operator** `|>` (a vertical bar followed by a greater-than sign). Let's start by seeing a reformulation of the code above with pipes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> filter(lifeExp < 50, year > 2000) |> arrange(desc(pop)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 42 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Nigeria Africa 2007 46.9 135031164 2014. 2 Nigeria Africa 2002 46.6 119901274 1615. 3 Congo, Dem. Rep. Africa 2007 46.5 64606759 278. 4 Congo, Dem. Rep. Africa 2002 45.0 55379852 241. 5 South Africa Africa 2007 49.3 43997828 9270. 6 Tanzania Africa 2002 49.7 34593779 899. 7 Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.8 31889923 975. 8 Afghanistan Asia 2002 42.1 25268405 727. 9 Uganda Africa 2002 47.8 24739869 928. 10 Mozambique Africa 2007 42.1 19951656 824. # ℹ 32 more rows ``` ::: ::: What happened here? We took the `gapminder` data frame, sent ("piped") it into the `filter()` function, whose output in turn was piped into the `arrange()` function. You can think of the pipe as **"then"**: take `gapminder`, _then_ filter, _then_ arrange. When using the pipe, you no longer specify the input data frame with the `.data` argument, because the function now gets its input data via the pipe (specifically, the input goes to the function's first argument by default). ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple'} Using pipes involves less typing and is especially more readable than using successive assignments^[ Using pipes is also faster and uses less computer memory. ]. For code readability, it is good practice to always start a new line after a pipe `|>`, and to keep the subsequent line(s) _indented_ as RStudio will automatically do. ::: :::exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Challenge 3: Find the mistakes** ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Instructions This pipeline is supposed to find the 3 countries with the lowest GDP per capita in 1997, sorted from lowest to highest. It has two errors. Find and fix them: ::: {.cell autorun='false' caption='' exercise='find_errors'} ```{webr} #| autorun: false #| caption: "" #| exercise: find_errors gapminder filter(year = 1997) |> arrange(gdpPercap) |> head(n = 3) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='find_errors' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: find_errors #| check: true if ( identical( .result, gapminder |> filter(year == 1997) |> arrange(gdpPercap) |> head(n = 3) ) ) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Nice work, that is the correct answer!") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's incorrect, sorry.") } ``` ::: #### {{< fa circle-check >}} Solution **The two errors are:** - Line 1: Missing pipe `|>` after gapminder - Line 2: Should use `==` (not `=`) to test for equality **Corrected code:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> filter(year == 1997) |> arrange(gdpPercap) |> head(n = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 3 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Congo, Dem. Rep. Africa 1997 42.6 47798986 312. 2 Myanmar Asia 1997 60.3 43247867 415 3 Burundi Africa 1997 45.3 6121610 463. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Challenge 4: Find the extremes** Using `filter()`, `arrange()`, and the pipe (`|>`), answer the following questions about the gapminder dataset: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Instructions A) Which African country had the highest life expectancy in 2002? #### {{< fa circle-check >}} Solution We'll use the same trick with `head()` like in the exercise above to _only_ see the top 1 country, but this is not strictly necessary: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> filter(continent == "Africa", year == 2002) |> arrange(desc(lifeExp)) |> head(n = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Reunion Africa 2002 75.7 743981 6316. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Instructions B) What was the smallest population recorded in Asia across all years? #### {{< fa circle-check >}} Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> filter(continent == "Asia") |> arrange(pop) |> head(n = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Bahrain Asia 1952 50.9 120447 9867. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## `mutate()` So far, we've focused on functions that subset and reorganize data frames. But you haven't seen how you can _change the data_ or _compute derived data_. This can be done with the `mutate()` function. For example, to create a new column with population sizes in millions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a new column 'pop_million' by dividing 'pop' by a million: gapminder |> mutate(pop_million = pop / 10^6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 7 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap pop_million 1 Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.8 8425333 779. 8.43 2 Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.3 9240934 821. 9.24 3 Afghanistan Asia 1962 32.0 10267083 853. 10.3 4 Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.0 11537966 836. 11.5 5 Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.1 13079460 740. 13.1 6 Afghanistan Asia 1977 38.4 14880372 786. 14.9 7 Afghanistan Asia 1982 39.9 12881816 978. 12.9 8 Afghanistan Asia 1987 40.8 13867957 852. 13.9 9 Afghanistan Asia 1992 41.7 16317921 649. 16.3 10 Afghanistan Asia 1997 41.8 22227415 635. 22.2 # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: To _modify_ an existing column rather than adding a new one, simply "assign back to the same name": ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Change the unit of the 'pop' column: gapminder |> mutate(pop = pop / 10^6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.8 8.43 779. 2 Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.3 9.24 821. 3 Afghanistan Asia 1962 32.0 10.3 853. 4 Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.0 11.5 836. 5 Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.1 13.1 740. 6 Afghanistan Asia 1977 38.4 14.9 786. 7 Afghanistan Asia 1982 39.9 12.9 978. 8 Afghanistan Asia 1987 40.8 13.9 852. 9 Afghanistan Asia 1992 41.7 16.3 649. 10 Afghanistan Asia 1997 41.8 22.2 635. # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: :::exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Challenge 5: Absolute GDP** ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Instructions Use `mutate()` to create a new column `gdp_billion` that has the **absolute** GDP (i.e., not relative to population size) in **units of billions**. ::: {.cell autorun='false' caption='' exercise='abs_gdp'} ```{webr} #| autorun: false #| caption: "" #| exercise: abs_gdp gapminder |> mutate(______) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='abs_gdp' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: abs_gdp #| check: true if ( identical( .result, gapminder |> mutate(gdp_billion = gdpPercap * pop / 10^9) ) ) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Nice work, that is the correct answer!") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's incorrect, sorry.") } ``` ::: #### {{< fa lightbulb >}} Hints ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> mutate(gdp_billion = gdpPercap * ______ / ______) ``` ::: #### {{< fa circle-check >}} Solution You need to do two things, which can be combined into a single line: 1. Make the GDP absolute by multiplying by the population size: `gdpPercap * pop` 2. Change the unit of the absolute GDP to billions by dividing by a billion: ` / 10^9` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> mutate(gdp_billion = gdpPercap * pop / 10^9) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1,704 × 7 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap gdp_billion 1 Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.8 8425333 779. 6.57 2 Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.3 9240934 821. 7.59 3 Afghanistan Asia 1962 32.0 10267083 853. 8.76 4 Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.0 11537966 836. 9.65 5 Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.1 13079460 740. 9.68 6 Afghanistan Asia 1977 38.4 14880372 786. 11.7 7 Afghanistan Asia 1982 39.9 12881816 978. 12.6 8 Afghanistan Asia 1987 40.8 13867957 852. 11.8 9 Afghanistan Asia 1992 41.7 16317921 649. 10.6 10 Afghanistan Asia 1997 41.8 22227415 635. 14.1 # ℹ 1,694 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## `summarize()` The final function _dplyr_ function we'll cover is `summarize()`, which computes **summaries of your data across rows**. For example, to calculate the mean GDP across the entire dataset: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The syntax is similar to 'mutate': = gapminder |> summarize(mean_gdp = mean(gdpPercap)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1 × 1 mean_gdp 1 7215. ``` ::: ::: The output is still a dataframe, but unlike with all previous _dplyr_ functions, it is completely different from the input dataframe, "collapsing" the data down to as little as a single number, like above. `summarize()` becomes really powerful in combination with the helper function `group_by()` to compute **groupwise** stats. For example, to get the mean GDP separately for each continent: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> group_by(continent) |> summarize(mean_gdp = mean(gdpPercap)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 5 × 2 continent mean_gdp 1 Africa 2194. 2 Americas 7136. 3 Asia 7902. 4 Europe 14469. 5 Oceania 18622. ``` ::: ::: `group_by()` implicitly splits a data frame into groups of rows: here, one group for observations from each continent. After that, operations like in `summarize()` will happen separately for each group, which is how we ended up with per-continent means. :::exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} **Challenge 6: Mean life expectancy** ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Instructions A) Calculate the average life expectancy for each country and store the result in a new dataframe. ::: {.cell autorun='false' caption='' exercise='life_exp'} ```{webr} #| autorun: false #| caption: "" #| exercise: life_exp gapminder |> ______ |> ______ ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='life_exp' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: life_exp #| check: true if ( identical( .result, lifeExp_bycountry <- gapminder |> group_by(country) |> summarize(mean_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp)) ) ) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Nice work, that is the correct answer!") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's incorrect, sorry.") } ``` ::: #### {{< fa lightbulb >}} Hints ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lifeExp_bycountry <- gapminder |> group_by(______) |> summarize(mean_lifeExp = ______) ``` ::: #### {{< fa circle-check >}} Solution First, create a dataframe with the mean life expectancy by country: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lifeExp_bycountry <- gapminder |> group_by(country) |> summarize(mean_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### {{< fa list-check >}} Instructions B) Use the dataframe you just created to find out which country has the longest average life expectancy and which has the shortest. #### {{< fa circle-check >}} Solution Arrange the dataframe in two directions to see the countries with the longest and shortest life expectancy. You could optionally pipe into `head()` to only see the top `n`, here top 1: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lifeExp_bycountry |> arrange(mean_lifeExp) |> head(n = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1 × 2 country mean_lifeExp 1 Sierra Leone 36.8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lifeExp_bycountry |> arrange(desc(mean_lifeExp)) |> head(n = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1 × 2 country mean_lifeExp 1 Iceland 76.5 ``` ::: ::: So, **Sierra Leone** has the shortest average life expectancy (36.8 years), and **Iceland** has the longest average life expectancy (76.5 years). ::: :::
